objectives.en: Describe the findings of the 1968 X-ray

narration.en: How can you look inside a body that is 3,300 years old without touching it? With an X-ray machine, and later with something far better.

body.en: In 1968, more than forty years after Carter, an anatomist X-rayed the mummy. The pictures revealed something startling: the breastbone and the front ribs were missing. This discovery added new questions about how Tut had died and how his body had been treated.

points.en: Raised new questions about his death

Let us compare the 1968 X-ray with the 2005 CT scan.

say.en: Let us compare the two ways of looking inside the mummy.
An X-ray gives a few flat images; the CT scan took about 1,700 slices.
The CT slices combine into a three-dimensional view.
The X-ray showed missing ribs; the CT scan showed the body in detail.
An anatomist did the X-ray; Zahi Hawass led the CT scan.

body.en: On 5 January 2005, the Egyptian archaeologist Zahi Hawass led a team that took the mummy from its tomb and passed it through a CT (computed tomography) scanner set up in a trailer nearby. The scanner made about 1,700 cross-section X-ray images that could be combined into a detailed three-dimensional view of the body. Work was briefly held up when a cooling fan in the machine failed in the dusty desert, but it was fixed and the scan was completed. The aim was to learn more about how Tut lived and died.

problem.en: How was the CT scan of 2005 an improvement on the X-ray of 1968?

steps.en: An X-ray gives only a few flat pictures.
The CT scanner took about 1,700 cross-section images.
These combine into a detailed 3-D view, without damaging the body.

answer.en: The 1968 X-ray produced only a few flat images. The 2005 CT scan took about 1,700 cross-section images that could be combined into a detailed three-dimensional picture of the body, giving far more information without harming the mummy.

body.en: Remember Tut's modern story in three dates: F-X-S. Found in 1922 (Carter), X-rayed in 1968 (an anatomist), Scanned in 2005 (Hawass). Each step looks deeper with less damage.
